q: The paper's RASTtk CDS count for UFLA258 is 3,949 while the deposited GenBank NCBI-PGAP annotation gives 3,813 for the same genome — a 3.4% gap. Which annotation is the right ground truth for comparative-genomics count claims across the 115-genome cohort, and how would using one vs the other shift the paper's 'CDS range 3,683–4,744' and PCA clustering?
basis: Observed directly in this replication (report/evidence/genome_stats.json shows 3,813 CDS from GenBank; paper reports 3,949 from PATRIC/RASTtk on the same assembly). Prokka-fast in-house gave 3,929 gene features — three tools, three different counts on identical sequence. This is a real gene-model calling disagreement that propagates into every downstream CDS-count-based comparison the paper makes.
next_steps: Re-annotate the 5 genomes here with (a) RASTtk-via-BV-BRC service, (b) NCBI PGAP-2024, (c) prokka --full-mode, and (d) bakta v1.9+ using the same input FASTA. Compare CDS-count distributions, functional-category coverage, and how any of the paper's cross-strain rankings (which strains have most/fewest genes) change under each tool.

q: antiSMASH v8.0.4 finds 13 BGC regions in UFLA258; the paper's antiSMASH 4.0.2 found 12. Is the extra region a real cluster now detectable due to improved rules, or an over-split of a region that v4 correctly merged?
basis: Direct antiSMASH v8 output in this replication (report/evidence/UFLA258_BGC_kcb_summary.json) — 13 regions, with region 6 and region 10 both KCB-hitting bacillaene/difficidin, hinting at potential over-splitting of one biological cluster.
next_steps: Containerise antiSMASH 4.0.2 (docker antismash/standalone:4.0.2) and rerun on UFLA258 with identical input; align region coordinates between v4 and v8 output; identify the one extra region and manually curate it against MIBiG references. If it's a real new BGC, backfill the paper's BGC counts across the whole 105-strain cohort — the paper's '12 groups' summary claim may be an underestimate.

q: The paper's dDDH values were computed with JspeciesWS (paper's methods) but were not re-computed here — only ANI (fastANI). Do modern dDDH implementations (TYGS 2024, GGDC 3.0) still support the paper's 70% same-species cutoff calls on the boundary strains, or are there strains where fastANI-≥95%-same-species conflicts with dDDH-<70%-different-species?
basis: The paper explicitly relies on the AND of both metrics (ANI≥95% AND dDDH≥70%) to make each of the 19 reclassification calls; this replication only re-verified the ANI leg. Boundary-strain flips between these two indices are a known problem in the microbial-taxonomy literature but the paper does not report per-strain agreement rates.
next_steps: Submit the 5-genome set (plus, ideally, the 19 reclassified strains named in supplementary table S1) to TYGS (https://tygs.dsmz.de) and GGDC 3.0; produce a scatter of ANI-vs-dDDH per pair; count strains where the two metrics disagree on species assignment at the paper's cutoffs; flag any of the paper's 19 reclassification calls that would flip under a dDDH-first policy.

q: Paper reports >85% CRISPR/Cas prevalence in B. velezensis vs ~33% in B. amyloliquefaciens. Is this a real ecological / genome-defense difference or a small-sample artefact (n=9 completes for amyloliquefaciens in 2019, vs ~200+ draft-plus-complete assemblies available now)?
basis: Sample-size asymmetry is explicit in the paper text ('due to the low number of genomes of this species, little can be inferred at this time'). CRISPR-array count was in our analysis plan but minced was not installed on uicgpu, and the 5-genome sample here is too small to test the ratio.
next_steps: Fetch all current *B. amyloliquefaciens* + *B. velezensis* NCBI assemblies (drafts + completes, ~2,000+ combined by 2026); run CRISPRCasFinder v4 on each; report CRISPR/Cas prevalence with 95% CI per species and per isolation-source subgroup (soil vs food vs plant-rhizosphere). Test whether the paper's soil-biased *B. velezensis* set is confounded with high CRISPR prevalence (soil = more phage pressure).

q: Paper argues UCMB5113 (deposited as 'B. amyloliquefaciens subsp. plantarum', HG328254) is actually B. velezensis — a claim this replication independently confirms (ANI 98.75% to FZB42, 4.6% above DSM7). Yet as of 2026, UCMB5113's GenBank organism field still reads 'B. amyloliquefaciens subsp. plantarum'. Why hasn't the paper's evidence-based reclassification propagated to NCBI Taxonomy / LPSN, and what fraction of the 19 reclassifications the paper called for have been fixed vs still mislabelled?
basis: Verified directly in this replication: pulled HG328254.1 header still reads 'Bacillus amyloliquefaciens subsp. plantarum UCMB5113'. The paper's central taxonomic contribution has not been operationalised in the reference databases seven years later — this is a real 'valid science, no infrastructure propagation' gap.
next_steps: Cross-reference the 19 strains from paper supplementary table S1 against current (2026) NCBI Taxonomy, LPSN, and BacDive records; report the propagation matrix (fixed / partially fixed / unfixed); identify the responsible curation pipeline for each database; write a short LPSN 'valid publications' correspondence proposing formal reclassification for any strains still mislabelled 7 years post-publication. Downstream impact estimate: any BV-BRC or PATRIC pipeline that keys off 'organism' string rather than ANI-clusters will silently misclassify these 19 strains.
